lines.speaker: Menippus
lines.text: Tiresias, even if you are blind, that is no longer very easy to tell. All our eyes are equally empty now—just the sockets left. The rest of it would not let you say which one used to be Phineus and which one Lynceus.

lines.speaker: Menippus
lines.text: Still, I know from the poets that you were a prophet, and that you alone managed both versions: man and woman. So, by the gods, tell me: which life did you find more pleasant? When you were a man, or was the female one better?

lines.speaker: Tiresias
lines.text: By far the female one, Menippus. Less trouble. Women rule the men, and they do not have to go to war, or stand on the battlements, or wrangle in the assembly, or be cross-examined in court.

lines.speaker: Menippus
lines.text: You have not heard Euripides’ Medea, then, Tiresias? What she says in pity for womankind—how wretched they are, and what an unbearable business the pain of childbirth is?

lines.speaker: Menippus
lines.text: But tell me—those iambics of Medea have reminded me—did you ever give birth, when you were a woman, or did you spend that whole life barren and childless?

lines.speaker: Tiresias
lines.text: Why are you asking me that, Menippus?

lines.speaker: Menippus
lines.text: No difficult reason, Tiresias. Just answer, if it is not too much trouble.

lines.speaker: Tiresias
lines.text: I was not barren. But I never actually gave birth.

lines.speaker: Menippus
lines.text: That will do. I only wanted to know whether you had a womb as well.

lines.speaker: Menippus
lines.text: And over time did the womb disappear, and the female part close up, and the breasts detach, and the male part sprout, and did you grow a beard? Or did you turn up as a man all at once, straight from being a woman?

lines.speaker: Tiresias
lines.text: I do not see what you are driving at with this question. You seem to me to disbelieve that it happened this way.

lines.speaker: Menippus
lines.text: Well, should one not disbelieve things like this, Tiresias? Should one accept them like some halfwit, without examining whether they are possible or not?

lines.speaker: Tiresias
lines.text: So you do not believe the other stories either, then, when you hear that certain women became birds, or trees, or animals—Aedon, or Daphne, or Lycaon’s daughter?

lines.speaker: Menippus
lines.text: If I ever run into them too, I will find out what they have to say for themselves. But you, my excellent fellow—when you were a woman, did you prophesy then as well, as you did later? Or did you learn to be a man and a prophet at the same time?

lines.speaker: Tiresias
lines.text: You see? You know nothing at all about my story. I once settled a dispute between the gods; Hera blinded me, and Zeus consoled me for the disaster with the gift of prophecy.

lines.speaker: Menippus
lines.text: Still got a few lies left, Tiresias? Well, that is professional conduct for prophets. You people have a habit of saying nothing sound.
